title: Rork Alternatives That Are Actually Better
summary: Rork alternatives sorted by who gets your app into the App Store and Google Play: Bitrig, Vibecode, FlutterFlow, Expo, Newly and more, priced and compared.
body_markdown:
Key takeaways:


- Rork's FAQ says it sends an iPhone build to Apple's App Review when you confirm (its docs stop at TestFlight and leave the product page to you), so the stronger reasons to switch are credits, price and stack.
- Three of the nine tools after ours, Bitrig, Vibecode and FlutterFlow, say without contradicting themselves that they submit to Apple's review for you, and only FlutterFlow's new AI builder claims the same for Google Play.
- Expo's free plan is the only $0 route here that uploads to both stores, though you bring your own coding agent and press submit yourself.
- Rork charges $20 to $1,800 a month outside India, with no yearly option, and its docs and pricing page disagree on which plan a new account gets.


Most Rork alternatives lists are written by a competitor that ranks itself first, and at least one still calls Rork a React Native tool. New Rork projects are native Swift for iPhone and Kotlin for Android, and Rork's FAQ says it submits to Apple's review on your say-so, though its iPhone docs describe an upload to App Store Connect and TestFlight, with the product page and review left for you to finish. Most rivals stop at that upload.


So "better" here means better for a named reader, such as someone who wants React Native back or credits that roll over. What sorts this list is who actually gets the app into the App Store and Google Play.


We put[Awesomic](https://www.awesomic.com/) first because it's our product, though it builds no native app, so read its Cons before anything else. Then come the tools whose own pages say, without contradicting themselves, that they send your app to Apple's review, then those that upload the build and leave the submit button to you.


Inside each group, the lowest month-to-month price on a plan with App Store publishing goes first, counting only the vendor's own fee and not an AI subscription you bring, and a tie goes to the tool that reaches more stores. Plan names and prices are as each vendor showed them on November 13, 2026.


## What pushes people off Rork


Rork is strong on store publishing, so people leave for other reasons, which its docs, FAQ and user threads spell out.


### Credits that burn on failed builds


Each message costs "what its work costs", and the iOS simulator burns 0.2 credits a minute. Rork's FAQ says iOS build time costs credits even when "the build fails", and plan credits don't carry over. Top-ups cost $0.22 a credit.


At least one user hit the wall before launch. In an[r/iOSProgramming thread on Rork Max](https://www.reddit.com/r/iOSProgramming/comments/1racv3n/how_is_everyone_feeling_about_rork_max_oneshot/) from February 2026, one commenter had "already run out of credits" before a first version, and another said it's "no where near 2 clicks" to reach the App Store. That's anecdotal Reddit evidence, but the credit rules are on Rork's own pages.


### Two price lists that disagree


Rork's paid plans run from $20 to $1,800 a month, monthly only. Its docs, updated November 11, 2026, say accounts opened since August 4, 2026 get one paid plan, Rork Max, at every price point, while the public pricing page still shows a $20 Pro tier and Max from $200. The FAQ adds that prices "can vary by account and region".


### No more React Native for new projects


Rork's docs say you "can no longer create Expo (React Native) projects in Rork". New apps are Swift on iPhone and Kotlin on Android, "two separate native apps" in one project that the agent keeps in step, though "The two apps can still drift". Old Expo projects keep working.


Teams that wanted one codebase must look elsewhere, and if you'd also rather build visually, our[Thunkable alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/thunkable-alternatives) roundup covers the drag-and-drop side.


### Android, support and the Rork app


On Google Play, Rork uploads your Android App Bundle (AAB) to internal testing and can promote it to production from chat, but its docs warn "there is no rollback". Its FAQ still says you upload the AAB by hand, which lags the docs, and sets a limit on support: "We cannot fix individual code issues."


The Rork app itself has changed. Its original App Store listing no longer loads in US, UK or German lookups, and the new Rork Max App installs from a computer and is "rolling out to selected accounts".


## The best Rork alternatives compared


The last column asks, for each store, whether the tool sends your app to review, uploads it for you to submit, hands you a file, or doesn't build for that store. Going by its FAQ, Rork's own cell would read "Submits to review / Uploads to internal testing", though its docs stop at TestFlight.


Awesomic brings AI agents and vetted experts into one app. Start with a prompt to build a website, app, campaign, deck or video, then switch models or bring in a vetted expert without losing the project context. AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


Only one tool claims review submission on both stores, FlutterFlow's AI builder, launched on November 4, 2026, and even it leaves the first Google Play release as a draft. Bitrig and Superapp skip Android, so if Google Play matters, weigh that first.


### 1. Awesomic


**Best for:** Web apps before store apps


**Overview:** Our agents don't build native iPhone or Android apps, and Awesomic doesn't upload to App Store Connect or Play Console, so we don't replace Rork's store step.


What they do build is web apps and sites. They work on a cloud computer that belongs to your project, publish the result to a live link in one click, and carry on while you're away from your desk.


Progress shows up in our iOS and Android apps too. On iOS you describe what you want, watch the agent work, preview the result and return to your chats and files, though neither app builds store apps for you.


For a real native app, a person does the build. Dedicated expert is the only plan on our pricing grid listing mobile app development, and only 0.82% of the experts who apply pass our vetting, with a match in as little as 24 hours.


**Key features:**


- Agents running in parallel, every one in a separate chat, on shared project files.
- Models from Anthropic, OpenAI, Google and xAI on one bill.
- A shared memory of your brand, files and past decisions, plus 200+ templates.
- Desktop apps for Linux, Windows (x64) and macOS (Apple Silicon).


**Pricing:** Agentic plans run $19, $99, $199 and $499 per person per month for Light, Basic, Pro and Studio, and each price is that person's monthly AI budget.


For current Awesomic plans and capabilities, see[the pricing page](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**Pros:** Web apps live at a link in one click, Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode on one bill, a vetted developer on a separate plan, free expert rematches


**Cons:** AI-agent plans start at $19/month, and expert plans start at $1,799/month.[See current plans](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) .


**How to start using it:**


1. Decide whether version one can live on the web.
2. For a web app, pick Pro; for a native app, start on Dedicated expert.
3. Read the checkout total before you pay.
4. Describe the app in the chat, or brief your expert there.
5. Publish the web version and share the link.


**Why it's a good Rork alternative:** You test the idea on a live link first, and a vetted developer owns the native build when it's time for the stores.


**Final verdict:** Need an app in the stores this month? Stay on Rork, or pick Bitrig, Vibecode or FlutterFlow. Choose Awesomic when a web app is the first product, or when a vetted developer should build the native app.


[Get started](https://www.awesomic.com/pricing) on Pro to try the agents on your web version.


### 2. Bitrig


**Overview:** Bitrig is a Mac app that builds native Swift apps, and its biggest difference from Rork is who pays for the AI. It runs Claude Code and Codex out of the box, plus agents such as OpenCode and Cursor, on the Claude or ChatGPT subscription you already have.


Publishing stays in the app. Bitrig's July 16, 2026 announcement reads: "When your listing and build are both ready, submit for App Store review without leaving Bitrig." It builds for iPhone, iPad, Mac, Apple Watch, Apple TV and Apple Vision Pro, and it offers no Android build.


**Key features:**


- Your own Claude or ChatGPT plan instead of a credit meter.
- Real Xcode projects, with GitHub import and pull requests.
- Listing, screenshots, TestFlight and in-app purchases set up in App Store Connect.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0 with 10 daily messages, and you can export your code at any time. Pro is $15 a month on your own AI subscription or $25 a month on Bitrig's credits, with no annual price published.


**Pros:** The cheapest plan here that submits to Apple's review for you, at $15 on a Claude or ChatGPT plan, code export on the free plan, every Apple platform


**Cons:** Needs "An Apple Silicon Mac running macOS Sequoia or later", no Android, Free stops at 10 messages a day


**Who it suits better than Rork:** Mac-based iOS developers with an AI plan, since Pro then runs "as much as your AI subscription allows".


**Final verdict:** Pick Bitrig for Apple-only apps when you own a recent Mac and already pay for an AI plan.


### 3. Vibecode


**Overview:** Vibecode lets you choose the stack per project: a native Swift app for iPhone and iPad, a React Native and Expo app for iOS and Android, or a web app. That's the choice Rork took away when new projects stopped being React Native.


For native Swift apps, its docs show each stage on screen, from "Uploading to Apple" to "Submitting for review." Google Play is different: "Google Play submission is not a built-in step; export the Expo project and publish it yourself", and source download starts on Pro.


**Key features:**


- Swift or React Native, chosen when you start each project.
- A cloud iOS Simulator in the browser, so you don't need a Mac.
- An MCP server that lets Claude Code, Cursor or Codex work on the project, on every plan.


**Pricing:** Plus is $20 a month or $200 a year with $20 of credits and App Store submission, and Pro is $50 a month or $500 a year with source code download. Credits roll over while your plan stays active, though Vibecode calls its pricing tiers "experimental".


**Pros:** Credits that roll over, React Native still on offer, yearly billing that Rork doesn't publish


**Cons:** No built-in Google Play step, code download only from Pro at $50 a month, no native Kotlin option for Android


**Where it edges out Rork:** You can still start a React Native project.


**Final verdict:** Choose Vibecode if your first launch is the App Store and you want to pick the stack per project.


### 4. FlutterFlow


**Overview:** FlutterFlow launched an AI-native app builder on November 4, 2026 and renamed its visual editor FlutterFlow Studio, with one subscription covering both. The new builder's homepage makes the boldest store claim on this list: "Send it to Apple and Google for review with one press. FlutterFlow follows each store until it's live."


That claim belongs to the AI builder. Studio's older docs leave the last step to you: in App Store Connect you "Select Prepare for Submission, add the app assets and metadata, and then click Add for Review", and the first Google Play upload is an AAB you send to internal testing by hand.


**Key features:**


- One Flutter build for both iOS and Android.
- A backend, sign-in and analytics built in.
- FlutterFlow Studio, the separate visual editor, for hand-built Flutter apps.


**Pricing:** Free has no one-click store deployment, so publishing starts on Basic at $39 a month, or $29 a month billed yearly. Pro is $80 a month, or $60 a month billed yearly, and adds a push to GitHub in Studio. That plan grid is labeled for Studio, so check the AI builder's publishing gate when you sign up.


**Pros:** Apple review submission and a Google Play draft upload from one codebase, Studio's code download from Basic if you build there instead


**Cons:** Flutter rather than Swift or Kotlin, AI usage shown as "the percentage left" rather than in published units, the one-press flow is days old, the AI builder has no code export or GitHub push, and projects don't move between it and Studio


**What makes it a Rork alternative:** It's the one entry promising both stores from one press, though its docs say the first Google Play release lands as a draft you roll out yourself.


**Final verdict:** Choose FlutterFlow if you want both stores reached from one Flutter project and can test a brand-new builder.


### 5. Expo (EAS)


**Overview:** Expo isn't a prompt builder, and that's the point for developers who left Rork over React Native. Its AI page says: "Claude, Codex, and Cursor write the code. Expo gives them builds, Expo Simulators, submission, updates, and monitoring."


Submission stops one step short of review. On iOS, Expo Submit uploads the binary, and then you "log in to App Store Connect and submit the build for App Review." On Android it "places it in the track you choose", with a brand-new app's first release on internal testing by default. It runs from any OS, Windows and Linux included.


**Key features:**


- Expo MCP, so your agent can start builds, check submissions and reply to store reviews, even on Free.
- Expo Skills, including one for the app stores.
- Expo Launch, which takes a GitHub repo to TestFlight, with Google Play marked coming soon.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0 with 15 Android and 15 iOS builds and "Submit to app stores" included. Starter is $19 a month plus usage with a $45 build credit, and Production is $199 a month plus usage.


**Pros:** The only $0 route here to both stores, any operating system, your code in your own repo


**Cons:** You need a coding agent and an Expo codebase, builds beyond the plan are metered, Expo Simulators are in beta for existing customers only


**The case for switching:** You keep one React Native codebase, pick your own agent, and pay Expo nothing until your build count grows.


**Final verdict:** Choose Expo if you can drive a coding agent yourself and want React Native back with builds, not AI credits, as the meter.


### 6. a0.dev


**Overview:** a0.dev is a prompt-to-mobile-app builder on Expo, with Convex or Supabase behind the app. Its homepage promises "One-click app publishing: We'll handle the build, create your App Store Connect listing, and upload it for you."


The docs tell a fuller story: you create the Bundle ID and app entry in App Store Connect first, and after "Generate & Submit" you go to TestFlight and submit for App Store review yourself. Those docs cover iOS publishing only, and we found no documented Google Play flow, so treat Android publishing as unconfirmed rather than missing.


**Key features:**


- An AI agent that writes an Expo app with a Convex or Supabase backend.
- Built-in setup for in-app payments.
- Over-the-air updates.


**Pricing:** Pro is $20 a month with 100 credits, "Unlimited app builds", code export and a custom domain. Max is $200 a month with 1,250 credits, and a0.dev shows neither a free plan nor annual billing.


**Pros:** The same $20 entry price as Rork with code export included, unlimited app builds listed on Pro, a build uploaded to App Store Connect for you


**Cons:** Google Play publishing not documented, no free plan, you press submit on Apple's side


**Who should try it:** Founders who want an Expo app with payments and a backend at Rork's entry price, since a0.dev lists builds as unlimited while Rork charges credits for build time.


**Final verdict:** Pick a0.dev for an iPhone-first Expo app where Android can wait.


### 7. Anything


**Overview:** Anything, formerly Create, builds Expo mobile apps and websites in one tool, and a paid plan is required to build. For a Rork user, the draw is one Expo codebase where Rork now starts two native apps.


On iOS, "Anything handles the build and uploads it to App Store Connect", and you then install through TestFlight and submit for review. Android is newer: "Android publishing is in beta. Your app is uploaded to Google Play's internal testing track as a draft."


**Key features:**


- Expo mobile apps and websites from the same project.
- A built-in backend.
- Uploads to both stores from one flow.


**Pricing:** Pro 20k costs $24 a month, or $19 a month billed annually, paid as $228 up front. Max plans start at $239 a month, or $199 a month on annual billing, and climb to $1,079 a month, or $899 billed annually.


**Pros:** One codebase for iPhone and Android, web and mobile together, an annual discount


**Cons:** No free building, Google Play upload still in beta, you finish the listing and submit yourself


**What you gain over Rork:** A yearly plan at $19 a month, which Rork doesn't offer, and one project for the web and both stores.


**Final verdict:** Choose Anything if you want a single Expo project for web, iPhone and Android and can pay annually.


### 8. Newly


**Overview:** Newly is the renamed Natively, whose old site now redirects to it, and its v2 launched on September 15, 2026. It writes one React Native and TypeScript codebase and runs it in cloud iOS and Android simulators.


Its docs are precise about the store step: "An owner or admin ships an iPhone build to TestFlight, or publishes to Google Play internal testing ... You submit for review yourself." That's a step short of what Rork's FAQ promises, though Rork's own iPhone docs also stop at TestFlight.


**Key features:**


- One React Native and TypeScript codebase for both platforms.
- Cloud simulators for iOS and Android.
- A source ZIP and two-way GitHub sync for owners and admins.


**Pricing:** Newly Apex is $25 a month for 100 credits and $50 a month for 200, with larger credit tiers above that. No free plan appears on the pricing page.


**Pros:** Both stores on the entry plan, two-way GitHub sync, cloud simulators for both platforms


**Cons:** No free plan, you submit for review on both stores, only owners and admins can publish


**Reason to shortlist it:** Its $25 entry plan reaches Google Play as well as TestFlight, which Superapp's plan at the same price doesn't.


**Final verdict:** Pick Newly if you want React Native with your code synced to GitHub from day one.


### 9. Superapp


**Overview:** Superapp builds native Swift apps for iPhone, iPad, Apple Watch and Mac, plus a website, and its FAQ says it "does not build Android apps". That FAQ also promises "no Mac and no local Xcode required", the same footing as Rork's cloud builds.


Its pages disagree on the last step. The product page says Superapp prepares the signed build and listing "and submits for review on your behalf", but the help center ends with "Finish in App Store Connect", where you confirm the listing, territories and pricing before the version goes to Apple. We follow the help center.


**Key features:**


- A standard Xcode project you can export.
- Figma import on Pro.
- Local agents such as Claude Code and Codex on a Mac folder.


**Pricing:** Free is offered in most countries, with credits that expire at midnight UTC. Pro is $25 a month with 50 credits, "Automated App Store publishing" and 240 preview minutes, and Business is $50 a month with 110 credits, all billed monthly.


**Pros:** Swift with an Xcode export, no Mac needed, a free plan in most countries


**Cons:** No Android, 50 credits on Pro at "roughly one credit" per screen, two pages that disagree on who sends the app to Apple


**Where it helps most:** A Swift app for Apple devices built without a Mac, with the listing and screenshots prepared for you.


**Final verdict:** Choose Superapp for an Apple-only Swift app if you'd rather not touch Xcode, and plan the confirm step yourself.


### 10. CatDoes


**Overview:** CatDoes is an AI agent for Expo mobile apps and websites that keeps building after you close the browser. Before you submit, it runs a readiness report for the App Store and Google Play.


The store flow splits by platform. On iOS, "you can ask the agent to submit it directly to the App Store", but the release decision, TestFlight or public, stays with you on Apple's side, which is why it sits in the second group. On Android, "you can download it and publish it on Google Play yourself." Both need a Starter plan or above and an Expo account.


**Key features:**


- A store readiness report before you submit.
- Website-to-app import.
- A built-in backend, CatDoes Cloud.


**Pricing:** Free costs $0 with 15 credits and web deploys only, and Core is $20 a month. Store deploys start on Starter at $50 a month, or $42 a month billed yearly, with 200 credits.


**Pros:** A readiness check before Apple or Google sees the app, an agent that runs while you're away, a website-to-app import


**Cons:** Store deploys start at $50 a month, code export and GitHub sync start on Plus at $100 a month, Android is a file you upload yourself


**What sets it apart:** The readiness report, which flags store problems before a review does.


**Final verdict:** Choose CatDoes if a first submission worries you more than the monthly price.


## Who presses submit, and what happens next


Every store route here ends at the same gate, Apple's App Review and Google's checks, and the tools differ in how close they get you: group one presses submit, group two leaves it to you.


Apple's figures show why the last step matters. Its[App Store Transparency Report](https://www.apple.com/legal/app-store/transparency/2025/) for 2025 counts 9,100,620 submissions reviewed and 2,093,244 rejected, plus 387,087 approved after an earlier rejection. Apple notes apps "may be submitted to App Review multiple times before they are approved", so these count submissions, not apps, and a rejection can mean another round trip.


That round trip is why Rork's AI App Store Reviewer, which checks a build against the five sections of Apple's guidelines, and CatDoes's readiness report matter. Google filters at scale too: in its[2025 Play safety post](https://blog.google/security/keeping-google-play-android-app-ecosystem-safe-2025/) , Google says it prevented over 1.75 million policy-violating apps from reaching Google Play and banned more than 80,000 bad developer accounts.


Google also adds time. Rork's docs note that a personal Play account opened after November 13, 2023 must run 12 testers through a closed test lasting 14 days before production, and that's Google's rule, whichever builder you use. A web app needs no review at all, and our[Glide alternatives](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/glide-alternatives) roundup covers builders that publish straight to a link.


## What it costs to reach the stores


The cheapest plan that publishes to the App Store isn't always one that reaches Google Play, so here are both, monthly. Apple's Developer Program, $99 a year per Rork's FAQ, comes on top of every row.


Read the metered column before the price. Most of these tools sell credits, but only Vibecode keeps unused plan credits for as long as you stay subscribed, Bitrig's credit plan carries them over for one month, and Superapp's Pro lists a rollover without saying for how long. Only a0.dev lists unlimited app builds. FlutterFlow also charges per extra seat on Pro and Max, and our[FlutterFlow competitors](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/flutterflow-competitors) guide compares it with similar builders.


## Design the screens before you prompt


One Rork user's launch started from a designer's files, not generated screens. In an[r/vibecoding thread on Rork Max](https://www.reddit.com/r/vibecoding/comments/1rjx91m/rorkmax_looks_quite_compelling_as_best_ios_native/) from March 2026, one reply says they launched "a very polished app with Rork Pro" in "about two weeks", adding: "I had professional designers do the design work in FIGMA." It's a single Reddit comment and anecdotal, but it treats design as a separate job from the build.


Superapp's Figma import on Pro takes that route most directly. If you'd rather hand the screens to a person first, start with[hiring a mobile app designer](https://www.awesomic.com/hire/hire-a-mobile-app-designer) , then give the agent the result.


## How to choose by what you need


Pick by the reason you're leaving Rork, not by the longest feature list:


- For React Native with your own agent, use Expo's free plan.
- For a prompt builder that still writes React Native, try Newly, Anything or a0.dev.
- For Apple review handled on an AI plan you already pay for, use Bitrig on a Mac.
- For credits that roll over as long as you're subscribed, Vibecode is the one that says so.
- For both stores handled from one build, FlutterFlow's AI builder is the one claiming it.
- If a first rejection worries you, start with CatDoes's readiness report.


## Where to start this week


Settle the screens first with one of these[app design apps](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/app-design-apps) . Then build the screen you'd show an investor in two tools from different groups, say Vibecode and Newly, using the same prompt. Push each as far as TestFlight and count the steps you did by hand.


## FAQ


### Does Rork still build React Native apps?


Not for new projects. Rork's docs say new apps are native Swift for iPhone, Kotlin for Android, or React and Vite for the web, while existing Expo projects keep working. Paid plans export iPhone apps as SwiftUI Xcode projects and Android apps as Kotlin projects.


### How much does Rork cost?


According to Rork's docs, an account created on or after August 4, 2026 gets a single paid plan, Rork Max, from 100 credits for $20 to 10,000 credits for $1,800 a month, billed monthly. The public pricing page still shows Pro at $20 and Max from $200, so check which plan your account shows before you compare Rork competitors. The free plan only lets you design.


### Which Rork alternative submits to the App Store for you?


Bitrig, Vibecode for its Swift apps, and FlutterFlow's new AI builder say they hand your app to Apple's review. Superapp's product page says it does too, but its help center has you confirm in App Store Connect first. Expo, a0.dev, Anything, Newly and CatDoes upload the build and leave the release step to you.


### Can I publish an iPhone app without a Mac?


Yes. Rork compiles in the cloud, Vibecode runs an iOS Simulator in the browser, Superapp's FAQ says no Mac is required, and Expo submits from Windows or Linux. Bitrig is the exception, since it needs an Apple Silicon Mac. You still need an Apple Developer Program membership at $99 a year.


### Should I hire people instead of using an app builder?


It depends on who will fix the app after launch. Builders reach TestFlight cheaply, but credits, rejections and fixes add up, and Rork's FAQ says its support can't fix your code, so if nobody on your team can, budget for people. For the screens, compare[mobile app design services](https://www.awesomic.com/blog/mobile-app-design-services) and what they cost.
